lessons.title: Seneca Falls Borrows the Form
lessons.mainIdea: The Declaration of Sentiments reused the Declaration of Independence's structure, changing one premise to reach a new conclusion.
reading: In July 1848, about three hundred people gathered in a chapel in Seneca Falls, New York, for the first convention in the United States devoted to women's rights. Elizabeth Cady Stanton drafted the meeting's central document, and she made a decision that was itself an argument. Rather than invent a new form, she took the Declaration of Independence and rewrote it. The result, the *Declaration of Sentiments*, follows the original almost line for line.

The first premise is where the change is made. The 1776 text says all men are created equal. The 1848 text says all men and women are created equal. Everything else in the opening follows: rights that cannot be taken away, governments that exist to secure them, the right to demand a new arrangement when the old one fails. Then comes the list of charges, and where Jefferson wrote He has about the king, Stanton wrote He has about man in general: he has never permitted her to vote, he has made her, if married, civilly dead in the eye of the law, he has denied her a thorough education.

The form is the argument. By keeping the syllogism and changing two words in the premise, Stanton forced her readers into a corner. Anyone who accepted the Declaration of 1776, which in 1848 was nearly everyone, and who rejected the Declaration of 1848 had to explain what made the two cases different. Either the first premise did not really mean all people, in which case the founders' argument had a hidden exception, or it did, in which case the conclusion about women followed. This is argument by *parallel*: matching a new case to an accepted one so exactly that denying it means denying the original.

The tactic had costs. Some readers found the parallel too neat, and the demand for the vote was controversial even inside the convention; Frederick Douglass, who attended, spoke in its favor when others hesitated. But the document's logic outlived the room. For seventy-two years, until the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920, arguments for women's suffrage returned to Stanton's move: hold the country to its own first premise.

lessons.title: Douglass and the Fourth of July
lessons.mainIdea: Douglass argued that the Declaration's premises condemned slavery, and used the nation's own holiday to make the contradiction visible.
reading: Frederick Douglass escaped from slavery in Maryland in 1838 and became the most famous Black orator and writer in the country. On July 5, 1852, he was invited to speak in Rochester, New York, at a celebration of Independence Day. He began by praising the founders honestly. They were brave, he said, and their Declaration was a great document, and its principles were right. Then he turned. The holiday, he told his white audience, was theirs, not his. To the enslaved American, the Fourth of July revealed more than any other day the injustice he lived under.

The structure of the speech is the structure of this unit. Douglass accepts the Declaration's first premise: all people have rights no one may take. He then supplies grounds: the laws of slaveholding states treat the enslaved as men, punishing them for crimes, which proves the slaveholders themselves know they are men. If they are men, the premise applies to them. The conclusion follows by strict deduction: the nation's practice contradicts its founding argument. Douglass refuses to argue the premise, saying the point is too plain to need proof, and spends his force on the contradiction.

He also refuses a false dilemma. Some abolitionists, following William Lloyd Garrison, held that the Constitution was a proslavery document and should be rejected. Douglass had once agreed; by 1852 he argued the opposite, reading the Constitution's text and finding no word of slavery in it. The Constitution, he said, was a glorious liberty document when read plainly. This mattered strategically. If the founding documents were on the side of freedom, then abolition was not a rebellion against the country's principles but their fulfillment.

The rhetoric is fierce, full of irony and direct address, and students sometimes take the fierceness for the whole. It is not. Under the heat is a syllogism the audience already accepted, applied to a case they had excused. That is what makes the speech an argument rather than a lament. When you write in dialogue with a founding text, Douglass's method is the model: grant the premise, prove the case, and let the reader feel the conclusion close.

lessons.title: Lincoln Rereads the Declaration
lessons.mainIdea: Lincoln's major speeches argue from the Declaration's premise, using compression and balanced sentences to make the logic memorable.
reading: Abraham Lincoln practiced law in Springfield for more than twenty years, and his speeches show it. He argued the way a good lawyer does: pick the premise the other side has already granted, and build from it. His chosen premise was the Declaration's. In June 1858, accepting the Republican nomination for the Senate in Springfield, he warned that a house divided against itself cannot stand, and that the nation could not endure permanently half slave and half free. That is a deductive claim: a divided house must eventually become all one thing or all the other.

That fall he debated Stephen Douglas seven times across Illinois, from Ottawa to Alton. Douglas argued that the founders had never meant to include Black Americans in the phrase all men. Lincoln answered that the founders had stated a principle they had not yet lived up to, a standard set for the future. The disagreement was about the first premise's meaning, exactly where the chapter opening said every argument about the Declaration would be fought. Lincoln lost the Senate race and won the argument's future.

At Gettysburg in November 1863, in about two hundred seventy words, he compressed the whole case. The nation was conceived in liberty and dedicated to the proposition that all men are created equal. Notice the word proposition. Jefferson's self-evident truth had become a claim to be tested, and the war was the test. The speech ends by turning the audience's grief into a premise for action: the dead gave their lives so that the proposition might hold, and the living must finish the work. The logic is a chain, and every link is a single sentence.

His Second Inaugural, in March 1865, weeks before his death, is the hardest of the three, because it argues against his own side's certainty. Both sides prayed to the same God, he observed, and neither's prayers had been fully answered; the war might be a judgment on the whole nation for slavery, not on the South alone. Then the famous close: with malice toward none, with charity for all. The passage moves from a premise about shared guilt to a conclusion about how to make peace, and the *antithesis* of malice and charity fixes the conclusion in memory. Lincoln's speeches endure because their rhetoric is the shape of their reasoning, not a decoration on top of it.

lessons.title: How Later Writers Argued Back
lessons.mainIdea: Later writers engaged the founding texts by granting a premise, exposing a contradiction, or contesting a definition, and each move is a model.
reading: By now you have seen three ways to argue with a founding text. The first is to grant its premise and demand the conclusion, as Stanton and Douglass did. The second is to contest a definition, as Douglas did with all men and Lincoln did back. The third is to reject the text outright, as Garrison did with the Constitution, calling it a pact with slavery. Each move has a different relationship to the original, and each requires different evidence.

The twentieth century kept all three alive. In 1963, on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial, Martin Luther King Jr. described the Declaration and Constitution as a promissory note that every American was to inherit, and said the nation had defaulted on it for Black citizens. That is Douglass's move updated: accept the premise, prove the contradiction, demand payment. King's Letter from Birmingham Jail, that same year, argued with a different set of texts, the statements of moderate clergy, by granting their premise that law deserves respect and then distinguishing just laws from unjust ones. A student writing today should study these as arguments, not only as history.

Courts argue with the founding texts constantly, and their moves are the same three. A judge who reads the Preamble's general welfare broadly is contesting a definition. A dissent that says the majority has abandoned the framers' design is granting a premise and charging a contradiction. Even ordinary editorials do it: a column that opens with We the People and asks whether a law serves the people is running the Preamble as a warrant. Once you know the three moves, you will see them everywhere, and you will notice when a writer performs one badly, quoting a founder as decoration instead of as a premise that does work.

That last failure is the one to avoid in your own writing. Quoting the Declaration proves nothing by itself; the founders are not an authority whose words settle a question, and treating them so is an appeal to authority outside its field. What the founding texts offer is premises that most of your readers already accept. The work of the essay is to show that your conclusion follows from those premises, or that your opponent's does not. Douglass did not win by quoting Jefferson. He won by showing that Jefferson's own sentence, applied honestly, condemned the thing Jefferson's country did.

lessons.title: Your Argument, Their Premise
lessons.mainIdea: An argument in dialogue with a foundational text states the text's premise fairly, adds your grounds, and shows the conclusion follows.
reading: Here is the assignment this chapter has been preparing you for: take a foundational text and write an argument that engages it. Not a report about it, and not an essay that quotes it once for flavor. An argument that uses one of its premises, or contests one, to reach a conclusion about a question that matters now. The method has five steps, and they are the Toulmin parts wearing new clothes.

Step one: state the text's premise in your own words, fairly, so that a defender of the text would nod. If you are using the Preamble, say what promoting the general welfare means in ordinary terms. If you are using Federalist 10, say what Madison means by faction, using his definition, not a cartoon of it. A straw man of a founding text is the most common failure in this kind of essay. Step two: state your own claim, with a qualifier that marks its edges. Step three: supply grounds from the present, evidence about the actual question, using at least two of the four kinds and asking each its limiting question before you use it.

Step four is the hinge. Write the warrant that connects the founder's premise and your grounds to your claim, and then decide whether to state it. If it is something your reader will grant, keep it quiet. If it is where the disagreement lives, argue it directly, with backing. Step five: find the strongest reply someone could make using the same text, and answer it. Douglas answered Lincoln with the same Declaration; Garrison answered Douglass with the same Constitution. A foundational text can nearly always be read against you, and a serious essay shows it knows that.

Look at a short model. Claim: Chicago should restore its ward-level participatory budgeting programs, at least in wards that have used them before. Premise from the text: the Preamble makes the people the author of government and its purposes the measure of it. Grounds: reports from wards that ran the programs, a survey of participants, a public-finance expert on cost. Warrant: a process that lets the people direct spending toward their own stated purposes serves the Preamble's design. Rebuttal: Madison would warn that direct decisions invite faction, and the answer is that the budgets are small, the choices are local, and elected officials still hold the final vote. Write yours the same way. Grant the premise. Prove the case. Let the reader feel the conclusion close.

engaging a text's actual premises and claims rather than merely mentioning it
a process in which residents vote directly on how part of a public budget is spent

look.title: Read Against Yourself
look.text: A student's claim: the state should lower the voting age to sixteen, because the Declaration says governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed, and sixteen-year-olds are governed. The student has grounds from turnout studies in cities that tried it and an expert on adolescent decision-making.
look.prompt: Write the strongest reply an opponent could make using the same Declaration or Federalist No. 10, then write the student's rebuttal in two sentences.

check.q: What is the most common failure in an essay that engages a foundational text, according to the lesson?
choices: Building a straw man of the text's premise
check.why: Misstating the text's premise means the whole argument answers a cartoon rather than the real document.

check.q: When should the warrant be stated directly in the essay?
choices: When it is where the disagreement lives and needs backing
Only when the essay is about the Constitution
check.why: A warrant the reader grants can stay quiet; one the reader may doubt must be argued.

check.q: In the model essay, what does the rebuttal do with Madison?
choices: It answers his warning about faction with the small scale and final official vote of the programs
check.why: The rebuttal takes the strongest objection from the same body of texts and answers it on the merits.

review.q: In the Declaration's syllogism, what role does the list of charges play?
choices: Evidence for the factual second premise
review.why: The charges are grounds offered to prove that the king has aimed at tyranny.

review.q: Which change to the rough draft turned a religious claim into a logical one?
review.why: Self-evident presents the premise as something no reasonable person could deny.

review.q: Which sentence names the six purposes of government?
review.why: The Preamble lists union, justice, tranquility, defense, welfare and liberty.

review.q: What kind of argument does Federalist No. 10 use to reach the large republic?
review.why: Madison rules out every other cure for faction until only the extended republic remains.

review.q: What premise about people does If men were angels establish?
choices: That people can be trusted to govern themselves without controls
That people, including officials, pursue their own interests and need controls
review.why: The false condition points to the true premise: people are not angels, so government must control itself.

review.q: How did the Declaration of Sentiments make its case?
choices: By rejecting the Declaration of Independence
By contesting the definition of a republic
By copying the 1776 form and changing the premise to include women
review.why: Stanton's parallel forced readers to accept the new conclusion or admit a hidden exception in the old premise.

review.q: What did Douglass argue about the Constitution by 1852?
choices: That read plainly it was a liberty document
That it should be rejected as a pact with slavery
That it had no bearing on his speech
review.why: He broke with Garrison and read the text as containing no support for slavery.

review.q: What is the best advice for using a founding text in your own essay?
choices: Quote it in the introduction and move on
Treat the founders as authorities whose words settle the question
Avoid founding texts because they are old
State its premise fairly, then show your conclusion follows from it and answer the reply that uses the same text
review.why: The text supplies a premise readers accept; the essay must still do the reasoning and face the counter-reading.
